messages.subject: applying detection probabilities
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have a good set of point transect distance data from which I can calculate
the detection probability and effective detection radius etc of a given
species for a given observer in a given habitat.

I have found a second, more primitive, data set, from the same observer
studying the same species in the same habitat but on that occasion a fixed
radius plot was used and only observations within that radius were recorded.

Assuming all others things are equal (e.g. the same effort was made at the
points in both surveys), can I use the detection information from the first
survey to improve the density estimate from the second survey?

Thanks

Jeremy

SYMPOSIUM ON LARGE DATA SETS
November 6th., 2003
Amsterdam, The Netherlands
http://www.vvs-ssp.nl/symposium2003.html

Organization

Section Statistical Software of The Netherlands Society for Statistics and Operations Research

Program Committee
________________________________
Dr. Ruud Koning, Universiteit of Groningen
Prof.dr. Arno Siebes, University of Utrecht
Dr. Siem Heisterkamp, National Institute of Public Health and the Environment (RIVM)
Prof.dr. Patrick Groenen, Erasmus University Rotterdam

Large Data Sets
________________________________
Fifteen years ago, handling of large datasets, let alone analysis in them was a nearly impossible task for researchers. The data were often stored on tape, and even the process of reading the dataset into the memory of a mainframe was slow. Memory was scarce, and so it was difficult to save intermediate results. Such datasets were analyzed using either tailor-made statistical software, or self-written programs using routines from numerical libraries like NAG or IMSL. Maximum-likelihood estimation of non-linear models was non-trivial if not impossible, and researchers often had to be satisfied with one-step improvements over some consistent estimator.

Things have changed for the better, from a technical point of view.  Huge datasets are routinely available to researchers in different fields, like finance, marketing, biomedical sciences, particle physics, astronomy, life sciences, and social sciences. Datasets used to be large in the sense of containing many observations on a small number of variables. But nowadays, e.g. in the life sciences we are confronted with datasets with a small number of observations and a huge number of variables. Data can be transported on media that can be read by most personal computers, and the computing power on the desk of a statistical researcher is absolutely impressive. Instead of focusing on the mechanics of the analysis of datasets, researchers can focus on the actual statistical analysis. Thus the question has turned into: Now that we have a lot of data, what could we do with it?

This conference addresses the analysis of very large datasets, both from the point of view of a statistician who works with such datasets as well as the point of view of practitioners from various fields. By presenting several applications and tools available to a modern day statistical researcher, we want to show that large datasets offer unique opportunities for researchers to answer questions that were difficult to tackle before. The program committee is delighted to be able to present a selection of the top researchers on this topic.

messages.subject: Re: applying detection probabilities
messages.body_plain:
Jeremy,

This is simple to do.  Simply employ the usual detectability adjusted
estimator:

D-hat=n/(a*Pa-hat)

where Pa-hat is the estimated detection probability over a strip of area a.

Include the variance of Pa-hat in var(D-hat) with the appropriate estimator
as well.

The only caveat I would suggest is that you are explicit in the assumptions
that you make in applying the estimated Pa to the old data.  In particular,
that detection probability is assumed to independent of any other changes
between the two surveys (e.g., observer ability, changes in habitat,
average weather, etc.).   Given some caution, this is a good way to
salvage the older data set.

Good luck,
Aaron

messages.subject: Re: Questions about maps & stratification
messages.body_plain:
Hi Fernando, list,

Can't answer your first question I'm afraid, not being a GIS guy.  But as to
your second:

> >2.      We do boat-based line surveys for marine mammals in a relatively small
> >area, divided in two strata: inshore and offshore. We did 48 transect legs
> >during the summer and have analysed the data using DISTANCE. We got very
> >large values for %CV and 95%CI. Our problem, I guess, is that our sample
> >sizes are very modest (23 observations of bottlenose dolphins, 45 of harbour
> >porpoise and 25 of grey seals).  We have additional data taken from the same
> >platform and under similar conditions, but collected while not following
> >strict transect protocol (i.e.: while in transit to waypoints or during
> >whale-watching trips). Could we use this additional data as if belonging to
> >a third stratum, and ask DISTANCE to estimate the detection function
> >globally and the density per strata only? The sample size would be greatly
> >increased this way. Would this help to reduce the CV & CI? Is this legal? If
> >so, how do we handle the CV & CI when we want to add up the values on the
> >two important strata (inshore and offshore) in order to produce estimates of
> >abundance in the whole area?

Firstly, you should check what's causing the large CV.  Remember that there are
three components of estimation: detection function, encounter rate and expected
cluster size.  All contribute to the overall variance. You can see the
percentage contributions in the Analysis Details | Results, at the bottom of the
page with the title that starts "Density Estimates".  If there is only a small
percentage due to estimating the detection function then the procedure you
describe won't help much in reducing the CV.

Secondly, to decide whether it's "legal" or not, think about whether you're
violating any of the assumptions of the method.  Normally, our transect lines
are placed at random (or random systematic, etc), so that the density of animals
is uniform with respect to distance from the transect.  In your case for the
non-random effort, is there any reason to think that the density of animals will
not be uniform within the strips?  For example, are many of the non-random
transects parallel to the shore and close in, with density of animals increasing
rapidly as you go away from the shore, etc etc.  Also, are there any other
reasons to suspect a different detection function in these transects vs the
others (e.g., observers not paying so much attention, etc).  If not, then I
don't see a problem in combining them to estimate the detection function -- but
with so few data you're not going to be able to test the assumption that the
observations from the non-random surveys are compatible, so it's a leap of
faith.

Even if including the other observations isn't going to decrease the CV much,
you may want to do it to increase the sample size -- 23 is really getting pretty
small to be fitting a detection function to - even if the observation process
has a wide shoulder, etc...

One way to do what you want in Distance is to use the multipliers facility.
You'd fit a detection function to all the data and write down the estimated p
and SE p.  Type these in as multipliers and then do a second analysis using only
the strata you're interested in, fitting a uniform detection function with no
adjustments (effectively a strip transect) but dividing the density estimates by
the multiplier p.  This is documented in the online manual -- look in the index
under Multipliers and look at the bottom bit of the page where it says
Additional Uses of Multipliers.

You could also do it using stratification as you suggest, but then you'll have
to work out the variance of abundance for the whole area (when you add the two
important strata together) by hand using the formulae in Introduction to
Distance Sampling (see the section on stratification there for an example).

Cheers,

 - Len

--

messages.subject: Re: chimpanzee nest project
messages.body_plain:
Hi Cleve, list,

Sorry to take so long to reply to your question (appended below). (I'm assuming
no-one else replied off the list otherwise I guess you'd have forwarded a
summary to the list.)

To summarize your situation, you feel you have an inaccurate estimate of the
centre of the group, and an underestimate of group size even for groups of nests
quite close to the line.

This means that you shouldn't use the normal size bias methods in Distance --
these assume you have accurate estimates of group centre and that you accurately
count group size for groups on and near the line.

Since you recorded the distance to every nest discovered, I suggest that instead
you switch to analyzing each nest as a separate detection, rather than using
cluster size methods.  This would violate another assumption -- that detections
on a line are independent.  However the methods are incredibly robust to
violation of this:
- One effect of violation is to make it seem that you have too many independent
samples when estimating variance and degrees of freedom of the fitted detection
function.  But remember that this is only one component of the variance in
density, and usually a small component.  Variation in encounter rate is usually
the larger component, and this is estimated assuming that the line is the
sample, not the observation.  Also, if you use the bootstrap to get a variance
estimate rather than the analytic method, and you bootstrap by line, then
dependence of observations within lines becomes a non-issue for variance
estimation.
- A second effect is to make it seem you have too many independent samples when
using AIC (or other model selection statistics) to determine which detection
function model to fit, and when using GOF statistics to judge model fit.  Using
AIC alone, for example, you will tend to fit more adjustment terms than you
would if you analyzed the data as groups.  A solution here is to try analyzing
the data as groups and see what model you come up with, and then apply this
model (or one with the same number of parameters) to the data where you treat
nests as individual observations.  Probably won't make a huge difference to the
results however.

One possible issue is that when you saw a nest from the line, you searched
intensively in the area around it.  This leads to more survey effort, and
therefore a larger effective strip width, in higher density areas.  This
scenario is mentioned as a possible problem on page 131 of "Introduction to
Distance Sampling", but having thought more about it, we have concluded that it
should not cause a major problem.  This scenario can be seen as another case of
heterogeneity in detection probability (higher detection probability in higher
density areas) and distance sampling methods are quite robust to such
heterogeneity (the "pooling robustness" property), in contrast to mark-recapture
methods.

You mention "outliers" and "truncation".  In determinig the truncation distance
when you analyze the nests as individual detections, I would follow the usual
guidelines - see the Introduction to Distance Sampling sections 2.5 (Some
analysis guidelines) and 4.3 (Truncation).

Hope this helps,

 - Len

messages.subject: Re: chimpanzee nest project
messages.body_plain:
Hi again,

Another thought just occured to me re. model selection for individual nests:
remember that your actual number of independent observations the number of clusters
of nests you saw, not the number of individual nests.  This means the AIC used by
Distance will be fooled into thinking you have a larger sample size than you really
have.  I suggested fitting first to the nest clusters and then using the same model
or number of parameters for the individual data.  Here's an alternative: work out
the correct AIC by hand.  Distance puts out the log likelihood value for each model
it fits, so you can easily calculate the correct AIC as -2LnL + 2q where q is the
number of independent observations -- ie the number of clusters.  Having calculated
the correct AIC for each model, you can then do your own model selection.

Cheers,

 - Len

--

Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Centre for Research into Environmental and Ecological Modelling

messages.subject: Unsurveyable area in plot
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I am using radar to conduct point counts for a seabird (Marbled Murrelet)
flying around in the forest.  The problem is that "clutter" appears on the
radar screen so that some birds are not detectable.  Buckland et al.
(2001; section 6.7) has a short discussion about how to deal with this
situation, which involves correcting the pooled detection function for the
proportion of area that is not surveyable (which changes with distance).
However, this solution may not be applicable in my case because it is
important for us to estimate plot-specific densities (the relationship
between the amount of clutter and distance varies by plot).  Ideally, I
would implement Buckland's approach and estimate plot-specific detection
functions that were corrected for the amount of clutter, but I don't have
enough detections in each plot to do so.  Can anyone envision a situation
where the area of clutter is used as a covariate or corrected for in some
other way?

Much obliged for any assistance. ZP.

Z

messages.subject: Re: Unsurveyable area in plot
messages.body_plain:
Hi Zach, list,

An interesting application.  I don't know anything about radar -- is it true that
the probability of identifying an object (murrelet) declines with distance from
the point, in a similar way to detection functions based on sightings, aural
detections, acoustic, etc?  I'll assume so.  Also, I'll assume that you the
distribution of the "clutter" with respect to distance from each point is a known
quantity -- i.e. you can measure it from the radar screen and don't need to
estimate it.  Then, there's no reason why you can't apply the method you suggest
(formula 6.44 in the book) to your data, with a global detection function g(r) and
the effort function e(r) calculated separately for each point.

The only down side then is the usual problem of bias that occurs when you estimate
a detection function at one level (global in your case) and predict density at a
lower level (by sample).  Points at which birds were more detectable than the
average will have abundance estimates biased high and visa versa.  How can you
minimize this bias?  You need to come as close to a point-specific detection
function as you can (given the usual parsimony and reliability arguments).  If you
have enough data per point you could try point as a factor covariate.  If not,
perhaps you could group points into habitats (or some other thing that would
affect the radar detection function) and use that as a factor.  I don't know if
radar is affected by weather but a weather variable may help too.  etc etc.

I'll be interested to hear how you implement the estimation routine.  In theory
the distance analysis engine D4.exe could be readily extended to do the job, but
it would take a little bit of thinking about how to implement this in a general
and accessable way.

Cheers,

 - Len

--

messages.subject: Re: about combined estimation
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

Gustavo's message started a series of emails between him, Steve Buckland, Jeff
Laake and I so I'll summarize the outcome in case anyone's interested.

In Gustavo's case, he has density estimates for two seasons and he wants to
calculate a mean density over both seasons.  Note that the inference here will
be limited to the two seasons he sampled -- he's not going to make inferences
about the density in other seasons he didn't sample from.  In stats language
this means treating season as a fixed effect.

An alternative would be if he had density estimates from a (large) number of
time periods, spread throughout the interval of interest.  For example, if he
wanted to know average density over a whole year and he had sampled on 52 days
spaced at weekly intervals (i.e., a systematic random sample).  In this case,
the 52 strata (time periods) could be regarded as a random sample of all the
time periods in the population (the 365 days in the year), and in calculating a
mean density for the year he'd be wanting to make inferences about the days he
didn't sample as well as the days he did.  In stats language this means
treating time period as a random effect.

In both cases, calculation of mean density over strata is the same.  But the
calculation of variance is quite different.  (You can skip the next paragraph if
you don't want to know the details of this.)

Let stratum v have density estimate D_v, with estimated variance var(D)_v (by
variance I mean standard error of the estimate of D squared), and weight w_v
(for example if we weight by effort as Gustavo did).  Let there be V strata in
total.  For simplicity we'll assume the stratum estimates are independent (i.e.
no shared components such as estimate of f(0)) -- although the variance formulae
below easily generalize. Then the mean density over the strata is
D=sum(D_v*w_v)/sum(w_v)
For fixed effects the variance of mean density is a weighted average of the
stratum variances:
var(D)=sum(var(D)_v*w_v^2)/sum(w_v^2)
where w_v^2 means the weights squared.  See Introduction to Distance Sampling
section 3.7.1 for examples of this when the strata are geographic areas.
Confidence intervals can be calculated using the log-normal method given in
equations 3.72-3.74, and the degrees of freedom for the t-statistic can be
calculated using the Satterthwaite approximation for a sum given on page 90
(which takes into account the degrees of freedom in each stratum).
For random effects the variance of mean density is calculated using the standard
formula for the variance of a weighted mean, assuming the strata are replicates:
var(D)=sum(w_v*[(D_v-D)^2])/(sum(w_v)*V-1)
For an example of this in a slighly different context, see Intro to Distance
Sampling, section 3.6.2 (formula 3.87).  Confidence intervals are again
calculated using the log-normal method, but this time the degrees of freedom for
the t-statistic are simply V-1.

How does this relate to Distance?  Well the Distance analysis engine has the
option to do either of these two analyses when you are calculating mean density
weighted by effort.  But when I was constructing the graphical interface, I
didn't include the option to treat the strata as fixed.  So when you choose to
weight by effort in the interface, Distance assumes you want to treat strata as
replicates (i.e., random effects).

So, that explains Gustavo's results: Distance was treating the two seasons he
surveyed as if they were a random sample from a large population of possible
seasons about which he wanted to calculate the mean density and confidence
intervals about the mean.  The variance was calculated using the random effects
method I outlined above and the confidence intervals were calculated using a t-
statistic with 1 degree of freedom.  Clearly a sample size of 2 strata is not
large for making inferences about the mean density, which is why the confidence
limits were wide.  (Critical t-value for 1df and alpha=0.05 is 12.71 -- put that
into formula 3.73 (see text below the formula about using t rather than z
statistics) and you get wide intervals!)  Gustavo kindly sent me his project
file, and since I have a slightly newer version of Distance than him I reran his
analysis and got similar results:

        Estimation Summary - Density&Abundance

                         Estimate      %CV     df     95% Confidence Interval
                        ------------------------------------------------------
 Stratum: e
 Hazard/Hermite
                 DS      6.3979       25.32    59.15  3.8856       10.534
                 D       10.154       26.42    68.99  6.0479       17.047
                 N       1868.0       26.42    68.99  1112.0       3136.0
 Stratum: j
 Half-normal/Polynomial
                 DS      6.0202       25.61    38.94  3.6155       10.025
                 D       7.9224       27.31    48.91  4.6212       13.582
                 N       1457.0       27.31    48.91  850.00       2498.0

 Pooled Estimates:
                         Estimate      %CV     df     95% Confidence Interval
                        ------------------------------------------------------
                 DS      6.3035        2.59     1.00  4.5336       8.7643
                 D       9.5960       10.07     1.00  2.6783       34.382
                 N       1765.0       10.07     1.00  493.00       6324.0

I also ran the analysis treating the strata as fixed - which is what he wanted
to do.  This is what I got:

        Estimation Summary - Density&Abundance

                         Estimate      %CV     df     95% Confidence Interval
                        ------------------------------------------------------
 Stratum: e
 Hazard/Hermite
                 DS      6.3979       25.32    59.15  3.8856       10.534
                 D       10.154       26.42    68.99  6.0479       17.047
                 N       1868.0       26.42    68.99  1112.0       3136.0
 Stratum: j
 Half-normal/Polynomial
                 DS      6.0202       25.61    38.94  3.6155       10.025
                 D       7.9224       27.31    48.91  4.6212       13.582
                 N       1457.0       27.31    48.91  850.00       2498.0

 Pooled Estimates:
                         Estimate      %CV     df     95% Confidence Interval
                        ------------------------------------------------------
                 DS      6.3035       20.22    70.58  4.2290       9.3957
                 D       9.5960       21.71    78.74  6.2600       14.710
                 N       1765.0       21.71    78.74  1151.0       2706.0

As you can see, the stratum estimates are unaffected, as are the pooled point
estimates.  But now the degrees of freedom and confidence intervals are much
more reasonable.

I've changed the Distance interface to allow the option Gustavo wants to be
selected: there is now a "Strata are replicates" tick box on the Model
Definition | Estimate tab, which you tick for the first analysis and untick for
the second (it is ticked by default for backwards compatibility).  I've also
updated the help file to make it clearer what Distance is doing when you choose
the various options on the Estimate tab.  I hope to put out a new version of
Distance in the next few weeks and that will include this change.

So, thanks to Gustavo for helping improve the program through his question!

 - Len

Postscript:
If you're desperate to do this analysis yourself, you'll have to run the
analysis engine as a stand-alone DOS program.  Instructions for doing this are
in the program manual - look in the index under "Running analyses - running the
analysis engine as a stand-alone program".  To get the input specifications you
want, I suggest the following procedure:
- get a stratified analysis set up in the Distance interface
- then from the main menu, choose Tools | Preferences | Analysis and tick the
box "Debug mode"
- run the stratified analysis.  Distance will then produce an analysis engine
command and data file for you in your computer's temp directory (look in the log
tab of your analysis to see where Distance has put them).
- use some windows editor to edit the command file.
For the analysis where the strata are treated as replicates look for the line
Density=Stratum
and you want the options
Density=Stratum /Design=Replicate /Weight=Effort;
For the analysis where the strata are treated as fixed, you want
Density=Stratum /Design=Strata /Weight=Effort;
(Aside: one small difference you'll notice if you do this before I release the
next versin of Distance is that the N you get in the second case will be
different from the N I give above.  That is because in the engine you have, when
/Design=strata, N is calculated as mean denstiy * sum(area of strata); I have
changed it to give mean denstiy * (area of stratum 1) which is more in keeping
with the other possible options here, and is also what's needed for analyses
like Gustavo's).

--
